14:T1324,<p>You launch an EC2 and AWS hands it a public IP. You point a DNS record at it and get to work. Then you stop the box overnight to save money, start it in the morning, and the IP is different. Every link to the old one breaks.</p>
<p>The auto IP is <em>dynamic</em>. To stay reachable you need an address that doesn't move. Three ways.</p>
<h2>1. Auto-assigned public IP</h2>
<p>No setup, but <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/using-instance-addressing.html#concepts-public-addresses">AWS releases it on every stop and assigns a new one on start</a>. Fine for a throwaway box, useless for anything you need to find again.</p>
<h2>2. Elastic IP</h2>
<p>A fixed address tied to your account. Attach it once, point an A record at it, done. It survives restarts.</p>
<p>It used to be free while attached. Not anymore: since February 1, 2024, <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/new-aws-public-ipv4-address-charge-public-ip-insights/">every public IPv4 address costs 0.005 USD an hour</a> (about 3.6 USD a month), in use or not, and the <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/vpc/pricing/">VPC pricing page</a> still lists that price. So an Elastic IP is a small, fixed line item. Release ones you're not using, or you're paying for nothing.</p>
<h2>3. DDNS</h2>
<p>Keep the dynamic IP, put a <strong>name</strong> in front. A small client on the instance loops over two steps:</p>
<ol>
<li>ask "what's my public IP right now?" (the OS only sees the private IP because <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/VPC_Internet_Gateway.html#ip-addresses-and-nat">the internet gateway NATs it</a>, so the client asks an outside service or the instance metadata endpoint),</li>
<li>if it changed, tell a DNS provider to re-point the name at the new IP.</li>
</ol>
<p>So <code>myserver.ddns.net</code> finds the box again after the IP flips from <code>54.201.13.7</code> to <code>3.88.42.190</code>, once cached DNS expires. You connect to the name; the client chases the IP.</p>
<p><strong>Already own a domain?</strong> If its DNS host has no update API, the client can't update it directly: Squarespace Domains, for example, dropped the dynamic DNS that Google Domains had. So get a free DDNS hostname and bridge to it with one CNAME, set once and never touched again:</p>
<pre><code>your.domain.com  ──CNAME──►  myserver.ddns.net  ──(DDNS keeps current)──►  the live IP
</code></pre>
<p><strong>The catch.</strong> DDNS used to be the <em>cheap</em> option, because the auto IP it rides on was free. After the 2024 change that IP costs the same 0.005 USD an hour as an Elastic IP while the box runs. The only saving left is the stopped hours: the auto IP is released on stop and billed nothing, while <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/elastic-ip-addresses-eip.html#eip-pricing">an Elastic IP is billed whether attached or not</a>. Stopped 12 hours a night, that is about 1.8 USD a month. For that, you trade a fixed IP for a free name plus a client to babysit.</p>
<h2>Where Route 53 fits</h2>
<p>An <strong>A record</strong> maps a name to a fixed IP (<code>app.mysite.com → 54.201.13.7</code>). A Route 53 <strong>alias</strong> maps a name to an AWS <em>resource</em> (ELB, CloudFront) and tracks its shifting IPs for you (<a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resource-record-sets-choosing-alias-non-alias.html">alias targets are AWS resources, not a raw EC2</a>).</p>
<p>So with an <strong>Elastic IP</strong>, use a plain A record; it never moves. A bare EC2 has no alias target, so it only gets an A record to its IP, which is exactly why it wants a <em>fixed</em> one. And if an <strong>ELB</strong>, or <strong>CloudFront</strong> with a <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-vpc-origins.html">VPC origin</a>, sits in front, alias your domain to that and drop the Elastic IP entirely; AWS tracks the IPs.</p>
<h2>The takeaway</h2>
<p>A public IP isn't free just because it's attached; since 2024 every one is metered. So choose mostly by simplicity: a fixed Elastic IP for anything real, an ELB in front if you'll pay more to forget IPs, and DDNS only for hobby boxes that sit stopped often enough for a free name to be worth babysitting a client.</p>
<h2>References</h2>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/new-aws-public-ipv4-address-charge-public-ip-insights/">New – AWS Public IPv4 Address Charge (AWS, Feb 2024)</a> — 0.005 USD an hour per public IPv4, in use or not.</li>
<li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/vpc/pricing/">Amazon VPC pricing</a> — current price.</li>
<li><a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resource-record-sets-choosing-alias-non-alias.html">Choosing between alias and non-alias records (Route 53)</a> — alias targets are AWS resources.</li>
</ul>15:T115c,
You launch an EC2 and AWS hands it a public IP. You point a DNS record at it and get to work. Then you stop the box overnight to save money, start it in the morning, and the IP is different. Every link to the old one breaks.

The auto IP is *dynamic*. To stay reachable you need an address that doesn't move. Three ways.

## 1. Auto-assigned public IP

No setup, but [AWS releases it on every stop and assigns a new one on start](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/using-instance-addressing.html#concepts-public-addresses). Fine for a throwaway box, useless for anything you need to find again.

## 2. Elastic IP

A fixed address tied to your account. Attach it once, point an A record at it, done. It survives restarts.

It used to be free while attached. Not anymore: since February 1, 2024, [every public IPv4 address costs 0.005 USD an hour](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/new-aws-public-ipv4-address-charge-public-ip-insights/) (about 3.6 USD a month), in use or not, and the [VPC pricing page](https://aws.amazon.com/vpc/pricing/) still lists that price. So an Elastic IP is a small, fixed line item. Release ones you're not using, or you're paying for nothing.

## 3. DDNS

Keep the dynamic IP, put a **name** in front. A small client on the instance loops over two steps:

1. ask "what's my public IP right now?" (the OS only sees the private IP because [the internet gateway NATs it](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/VPC_Internet_Gateway.html#ip-addresses-and-nat), so the client asks an outside service or the instance metadata endpoint),
2. if it changed, tell a DNS provider to re-point the name at the new IP.

So `myserver.ddns.net` finds the box again after the IP flips from `54.201.13.7` to `3.88.42.190`, once cached DNS expires. You connect to the name; the client chases the IP.

**Already own a domain?** If its DNS host has no update API, the client can't update it directly: Squarespace Domains, for example, dropped the dynamic DNS that Google Domains had. So get a free DDNS hostname and bridge to it with one CNAME, set once and never touched again:

```
your.domain.com  ──CNAME──►  myserver.ddns.net  ──(DDNS keeps current)──►  the live IP
```

**The catch.** DDNS used to be the *cheap* option, because the auto IP it rides on was free. After the 2024 change that IP costs the same 0.005 USD an hour as an Elastic IP while the box runs. The only saving left is the stopped hours: the auto IP is released on stop and billed nothing, while [an Elastic IP is billed whether attached or not](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/elastic-ip-addresses-eip.html#eip-pricing). Stopped 12 hours a night, that is about 1.8 USD a month. For that, you trade a fixed IP for a free name plus a client to babysit.

## Where Route 53 fits

An **A record** maps a name to a fixed IP (`app.mysite.com → 54.201.13.7`). A Route 53 **alias** maps a name to an AWS *resource* (ELB, CloudFront) and tracks its shifting IPs for you ([alias targets are AWS resources, not a raw EC2](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resource-record-sets-choosing-alias-non-alias.html)).

So with an **Elastic IP**, use a plain A record; it never moves. A bare EC2 has no alias target, so it only gets an A record to its IP, which is exactly why it wants a *fixed* one. And if an **ELB**, or **CloudFront** with a [VPC origin](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-vpc-origins.html), sits in front, alias your domain to that and drop the Elastic IP entirely; AWS tracks the IPs.

## The takeaway

A public IP isn't free just because it's attached; since 2024 every one is metered. So choose mostly by simplicity: a fixed Elastic IP for anything real, an ELB in front if you'll pay more to forget IPs, and DDNS only for hobby boxes that sit stopped often enough for a free name to be worth babysitting a client.

## References

- [New – AWS Public IPv4 Address Charge (AWS, Feb 2024)](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/new-aws-public-ipv4-address-charge-public-ip-insights/) — 0.005 USD an hour per public IPv4, in use or not.
- [Amazon VPC pricing](https://aws.amazon.com/vpc/pricing/) — current price.
- [Choosing between alias and non-alias records (Route 53)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resource-record-sets-choosing-alias-non-alias.html) — alias targets are AWS resources.
16:T18dc,:T16d0,<p>在 AWS 開一台 EC2，它會自動拿到一個 public IP。把 DNS record 指過去，就可以開始用了。可是如果為了省錢晚上把它 stop，隔天早上再 start，IP 就換了，所有指向舊 IP 的連結都會失效。</p>
<p>自動配的 IP 是浮動的，要讓別人一直連得上，就需要一個不會變的位址。常見的做法有三種。</p>
<h2>1. 自動配發的 public IP</h2>
<p>不用任何設定，但 <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/using-instance-addressing.html#concepts-public-addresses">AWS 每次 stop 都會收回這個 IP，start 時再配一個新的</a>。用完就丟的機器用它沒問題，需要讓人固定找到的服務就不適合。</p>
<h2>2. Elastic IP</h2>
<p>Elastic IP 是綁在 AWS 帳號上的固定位址。把它 attach 到 instance，再設一筆 A record 指過去就好，重開機也不會變。</p>
<p>以前它只要 attach 在 instance 上就不收錢，現在要收了。從 2024 年 2 月 1 日起，<a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/new-aws-public-ipv4-address-charge-public-ip-insights/">每個 public IPv4 位址每小時收 0.005 美元</a>（一個月大約 3.6 美元），不管有沒有在用都算，而 <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/vpc/pricing/">VPC 價目頁</a>現在列的也還是這個價格。沒 attach 在任何東西上的 Elastic IP 也一樣計費，用不到的就 release 掉。</p>
<h2>3. DDNS</h2>
<p>DDNS（Dynamic DNS）的做法是保留會變的 IP，在它前面放一個<strong>名字</strong>。instance 上跑一支小 client，一直重複下面兩個步驟。</p>
<ol>
<li>查詢自己現在的 public IP。作業系統的網路介面上只有 private IP，因為 <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/VPC_Internet_Gateway.html#ip-addresses-and-nat">internet gateway 會替它做 NAT</a>，所以 client 要去問外部的服務，或是問 instance metadata endpoint。</li>
<li>如果 IP 變了，就通知 DNS 服務商，把名字改指到新的 IP。</li>
</ol>
<p>這樣一來，IP 從 <code>54.201.13.7</code> 變成 <code>3.88.42.190</code> 之後，等各地的 DNS 快取過期，用 <code>myserver.ddns.net</code> 就又能連到這台機器。</p>
<p><strong>已經有自己的網域了？</strong> 如果網域的 DNS 服務商沒有提供更新用的 API，client 就沒辦法直接更新它，例如 Squarespace Domains 接手 Google Domains 之後，就拿掉了原本的 dynamic DNS 功能。這時可以先申請一個免費的 DDNS hostname，再用一筆 CNAME 接過去，設定一次之後就不用再動。</p>
<pre><code>your.domain.com  ──CNAME──►  myserver.ddns.net  ──(DDNS 隨時更新)──►  現在的 IP
</code></pre>
<p><strong>不過 DDNS 現在能省的錢很少。</strong> 它以前是比較<em>便宜</em>的選項，因為它用的自動 IP 不用錢。2024 年改制之後，instance 開著的時候，這個 IP 跟 Elastic IP 一樣每小時 0.005 美元。現在只有 instance stop 的那幾個小時還能省，因為自動 IP 在 stop 時就被收回、不計費，而 <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/elastic-ip-addresses-eip.html#eip-pricing">Elastic IP 不管有沒有 attach 都照樣計費</a>。如果每晚 stop 12 小時，一個月大約省 1.8 美元。要省下這 1.8 美元，就得在 instance 上一直維護一支 DDNS client。</p>
<h2>Route 53 該用 A record 還是 alias</h2>
<p><strong>A record</strong> 把名字對到一個固定的 IP（<code>app.mysite.com → 54.201.13.7</code>）。Route 53 的 <strong>alias</strong> 則是把名字對到一個 AWS <strong>資源</strong>（ELB、CloudFront），資源背後的 IP 變了，Route 53 會自己跟著更新（<a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resource-record-sets-choosing-alias-non-alias.html">alias 的目標只能是 AWS 資源，不包括單獨一台 EC2</a>）。</p>
<p>所以用 <strong>Elastic IP</strong> 的話，設一般的 A record 就好，因為 IP 不會變。單獨一台 EC2 不能當 alias 的目標，只能用 A record 指向它的 IP，這也是它需要<em>固定</em> IP 的原因。如果前面有 <strong>ELB</strong>，或是用 <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-vpc-origins.html">VPC origin</a> 接到 EC2 的 <strong>CloudFront</strong>，就把網域 alias 到它們，Elastic IP 可以整個拿掉，IP 交給 AWS 追蹤。</p>
<h2>該選哪一種</h2>
<p>2024 年起每個 public IP 都計費。DDNS 跟 Elastic IP 只在 instance stop 的時候價格有差，就算每晚 stop 12 小時，一個月也只差 1.8 美元左右，所以在這兩種之間，價格不太會影響選擇。</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Elastic IP</strong>：設定一次就不用再管，適合正式的服務。</li>
<li><strong>ELB</strong>：把網域 alias 到 ELB，IP 變了由 AWS 追蹤，維運的人完全不用管 IP，但 ELB 本身也要另外計費。</li>
<li><strong>DDNS</strong>：要一直維護一支 client，比另外兩種麻煩。如果是常常 stop 的個人實驗機，為了 stop 那幾個小時省下的錢，多顧一支 client 也許還划得來。</li>
</ul>
<h2>參考資料</h2>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/new-aws-public-ipv4-address-charge-public-ip-insights/">New – AWS Public IPv4 Address Charge（AWS，2024 年 2 月）</a> — 每個 public IPv4 每小時 0.005 美元，不管有沒有在用。</li>
<li><a href="https://aws.amazon.com/vpc/pricing/">Amazon VPC 價目頁</a> — 現在的價格。</li>
<li><a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/Route53/latest/DeveloperGuide/resource-record-sets-choosing-alias-non-alias.html">Choosing between alias and non-alias records（Route 53）</a> — alias 的目標是 AWS 資源。</li>
</ul>8:["$","div",null,{"id":"root","children":["$","div",null,{"id":"main","className":"reading","children":["$","$L13",null,{"htmlContent":"$14","rawContent":"$15","base64Content":"$16","title":"Three ways to keep an EC2 reachable, and why DDNS barely saves money now","createdAt":"2024-10-07T22:43:00.000Z","updatedAt":"$undefined","tags":["aws","ec2","networking","route53"],"altHtmlContent":"$17","altTitle":"EC2 每次重開 IP 都會換，怎麼讓它有固定的位址","currentLang":"en","altLang":"zh","canonicalPath":"$undefined"}]}]}]
